blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we start on a football pitch in London, with a sixteen-year-old who collected three world records in one season.
Then we tiptoe into quiet homes in Japan, where scientists watched cats — and their owners' moods.
Ready?
Let's go!
Meet Max Dowman, a young winger at Arsenal, a famous football club in England.
At fifteen years and three hundred and eight days old, he stepped onto the pitch in the Champions League, the biggest club competition in Europe.
No player that young had ever done it.
It sounds absurd — but it really happened!
His second record was pure magic.
In a league match against Everton, the goalkeeper had run up the field, leaving his goal empty.
Dowman got the ball in his own half and ran — past one player, past another, sixty metres — then rolled it into the empty net.
The crowd erupted!
At sixteen years and seventy-three days, he was the youngest goalscorer in Premier League history.
In a cup match, he scored twice in one game — and on his first league match, he won a penalty to assist his team.
Then, when Arsenal won the Premier League title, he lifted the trophy at sixteen years and one hundred and forty-four days: the youngest champion ever.
Coaches say he is determined and careful — he trains hard and never stops learning.
A rising star for his club, and one day for his country too.
Now let's leave the noisy stadium and visit quiet homes in Japan.
Many cat owners say their cat makes them feel happy and calm.
But is that just a feeling — or can science measure it?
Scientists at Kyoto University followed twenty-nine cats and nineteen owners for a whole month.
No cages, no laboratories — just sofas, saucers of milk, and sleepy afternoons.
Each cat wore a tiny Bluetooth beacon on its collar, like a mini name tag that talks to the owner's phone, quietly measuring how close the cat stayed to its owner.
Scientists also tested samples from cats and owners, hunting for two body chemicals: oxytocin, the "love hormone" that grows when we hug and play, and cortisol, the stress hormone.
And what did they find?
When a cat's oxytocin was high, its owner's was high too — their bodies rose and fell together, like dancers following the same music.
Cats with more oxytocin had owners with less stress and fewer bad moods, and owners who stayed close to their cats felt brighter and full of energy.
Who cheers up whom — the cat, or the owner?
Nobody knows yet.
Maybe it is a circle of purrs, going round and round.
Here's today's idiom: "shoot for the stars." If you shoot for the stars, you set a big goal and try your best to reach it, even if it looks far away.
Max Dowman shot for the stars, and he caught three world records!
Here's an example: "Mia loves drawing, so she shoots for the stars and practises every day." What stars are you shooting for?
Let's think about today's stories.
We met a sixteen-year-old with three world records, and learned that cats and owners share happy chemicals.
Now, two questions for you.
First: which world record would you like to break one day?
Second: do you think your pet knows when you are happy or sad?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Keep practising like Max, keep cuddling your cats, and always shoot for the stars.
See you tomorrow morning!
